newsitem.title: USA: Republican leaders dangle tax cut promise.
newsitem.headline: Republican leaders dangle tax cut promise.

text.p: Republican congressional leaders on Sunday night said a tax cut would top their agenda next year if they won control of Congress, but Democrats warned such a cut would only benefit the rich.

In a mellow debate with many familiar themes, the leaders outlined radically different visions for the country as they scrambled to attract undecided voters in the remaining five weeks until the November 5 election.

Democrats presented their goals of tax cuts aimed at families, more funds for education, campaign finance reform, and environmental protection. Republicans said they agreed with these goals in principal, including more money for education, but intended to accomplish this with lower taxes and smaller government. Fighting illegal drugs will be one of their top domestic and foreign policy goals, Republicans said.
At stake, in what is predicted to be a very close race, is which party will control Congress, set its agenda and put its leaders in charge of powerful committees.

"The first thing we would do next year is give people general tax relief. Why do you want to keep all this money in Washington?" Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, R-Mississippi, said to Senate Minority Leader Tom Daschle, D-South Dakota and House Minority Leader Richard Gephardt, D-Missouri, seated across from him and House Speaker Newt Gingrich, R-Georgia.

Daschle responded: "Their proposal for tax cuts will be paid for by cuts in Medicare, the environment and education ... We want to do it for the middle class. You want to do it for people at the top."

Democrats have tried to make the election a referendum on Gingrich's conservative revolution, but the firebrand Speaker set aside his confrontation tendencies to present a mild face to the audience. But the issue was raised during the debate.

The economy dominated the discussion with Democrats harkening back to the record of the first Republican controlled Congress in 40 years and noting the Reublican revolution brought two government shutdowns, one of 27 days, as they pressed President Clinton to accept their budget cuts. Ultimately, compromise was reached when Clinton used his veto power to reject some of their plans.

"We will never, ever shut the government down," Daschle said. He charged the shutdowns cost the government $1.4 billion, far outstripping the $500,000 savings Gingrich noted came from his party's decision to end ice deliveries to lawmakers offices.

Gingrich said his party had learned from last year's budget experience. And, in fact House Republicans Saturday agreed to a bipartisan 1997 government budget that granted President Clinton $6.5 billion more for his education and domestic priorities. Lott will support its passage in the Senate Monday.
The plan holds goverment spending in 1997 at the levels set in the Republican budget.

The leaders sat across from each other at wooden desks with moderator Jim Lehrer of Public Television's "The Newshour" in between. Lehrer has been recommended by President Clinton and his Republican rival Bob Dole as the moderator of their presidential debates.

The setting was the reconstructed colonial Virginia House of Burgesses. On this site May 15, 1776 the colonial delegates voted for independence from Britain, providing the spark for the Revolutionary War.

On this night, however, the benches lining the walls were empty, a fact the leaders said contributed to the calm nature of their discussion. Gingrich said after the debate the format will likely make the presidential debates also, "milder and mellower" than previous presidential debates.
The only tense moment came when Daschle accused Republicans of conspiring with indusry to weaken environmental laws, which Gingrich hotly denied.

With 435 House seats and one-third of the 100 member Senate at stake, the political issues in each state and district are unique but have overtones of the national political battle being waged between Clinton and Dole.
Republicans pointed to their legislative successes in expanding health care and tax-deferred retirement accounts,in clean air and clean water legislation, telecommunications and agriculture.
